# Dental Implants in Hackensack, NJ


A permanent, natural-feeling way to replace missing or failing teeth. Planned in 3D, placed by a specialist, and designed to last for decades.

JUMP TO SECTION:

Show sections

1. What Are Dental Implants?2. Dental Implants at a Glance3. Ideal Candidates4. Why Us?5. Types of Dental Implants6. Dental Implants Process7. Recovery8. Frequently Asked Questions


## What Are Dental Implants?


A dental implant is a permanent replacement for a missing or failing tooth, built from the root up rather than resting on your gums or the teeth beside it. It replaces the whole tooth, not just the part you see.

Every implant has three parts. A small titanium post takes the place of the tooth root and is set into the jawbone. An abutment connects to that post and rises through the gum. A custom crown sits on top and looks and works like a natural tooth. Because the post fuses with your jawbone through a process called osseointegration, the implant stays firmly in place while you eat, speak, and smile.

Dental implants are used to replace anything from a single tooth to an entire arch, and they are the only tooth replacement that preserves the jawbone underneath. That is why, when the situation allows for them, they are considered the gold standard.


## Dental Implants at a Glance


What Dental Implants Give You Back

Dental implants are the only tooth replacement that behaves like the real thing, which is why they are considered the gold standard. What patients notice, from day one and years later:

Feel like natural teeth. Fixed in place, so nothing shifts or comes out.

Preserve your jawbone. The post replaces the root and stops the bone from shrinking.

Full biting strength. Eat what you want, chew on either side without thinking about it.

Designed to last. Decades for the crown, often a lifetime for the post.

What They Are Made Of

The implant post is titanium in almost every case, chosen because bone bonds to it naturally and it has decades of clinical research behind it. Zirconia is a newer, metal-free alternative that some patients prefer for aesthetic or biocompatibility reasons.

Titanium. The standard. Lightweight, biocompatible, extensively researched.

Zirconia. A tooth-colored ceramic option, useful in visible sites or for patients who prefer metal-free.

The crown on top is usually porcelain or zirconia, matched to the shade and shape of your other teeth.

How Long They Last

Well-placed and well-maintained dental implants are designed to last for decades, and the post itself often lasts a lifetime. The crown on top is a wear part, like anything you use every day, and may need replacement or maintenance over the years. What extends an implant's life most is not the material, it is good daily brushing and flossing, regular check-ups, and the skill of the specialist who placed it.

Are They Safe?

Yes. Dental implants have been in wide clinical use for over 40 years, with success rates around 95 percent when placed by a trained specialist, according to major long-term studies.

The surgery itself is a routine, focused procedure done under local anesthetic, with sedation available for patients who want it. As with any minor surgery, healing depends on general health and habits like smoking, which is why the consultation covers your full history before we plan anything.


## Who Can Have Dental Implants?


Most healthy adults are candidates for dental implants, and many people who were told no elsewhere still qualify here with the right preparation. Five things get checked at your consultation, each with a straightforward path forward if it needs work. A 3D scan gives us a definite answer.

01

Adult with a fully developed jaw

Implants are for adults, because the jaw has to have finished growing before a permanent post goes into it. Placing an implant in a jaw that is still developing can push a tooth out of position later or leave the implant misaligned. There is no upper age limit. Patients in their 70s, 80s, and 90s receive implants regularly and heal well, since what matters far more than age is general health, the quality of the bone, and how well you look after your mouth.

02

Enough bone at the implant site, or a plan to rebuild it

An implant fuses directly to your jawbone, so there has to be enough healthy bone in that spot to hold it. Bone begins to shrink the moment a tooth is lost, and the longer a gap sits empty, the more it recedes. This is one of the top reasons patients are told "no implants" by another office, and it is often not the whole story.

Your 3D scan measures the exact height and width of bone available at each planned site.

Small deficits are treated with focused grafting, sometimes done at the same visit as placement.

Larger deficits are rebuilt with a graft before implants go in, adding a few months to the plan.

Angled implant designs like All-on-4 can work with limited bone in the back of the jaw, sometimes avoiding grafting altogether.

If you have been told your bone is not enough, it is worth a second look with a proper scan.

03

Healthy gums, with any active disease treated first

Gum disease is the leading cause of tooth loss in adults, and it does not go away on its own. Because an implant sits in the same bone that gum disease attacks, any active infection has to be under control before implants can be placed. Signs of active disease include gums that bleed easily, receding gum lines, deep pockets around the teeth, and bone loss visible on x-rays.

The important part: a history of gum disease does not disqualify you. Even patients with significant past bone loss can go on to have successful implants once the infection is treated with deep cleanings, antibiotics, or periodontal procedures, and once ongoing maintenance is in place. What matters is that the disease is controlled and stays controlled.

04

General health that supports healing

Implant placement is a routine, focused surgery, and healing depends on the same things any other surgery does. Most healthy adults qualify, including patients with well-managed chronic conditions.

Well-controlled diabetes is usually fine. Uncontrolled diabetes with unstable blood sugar meaningfully raises the risk of implant failure and needs to be brought under control first.

Certain medications can affect bone healing, including some osteoporosis drugs and long-term steroids. We review your full medication list at consultation.

Autoimmune conditions and treatments are planned around case by case, sometimes in coordination with your physician.

Radiation to the jaw or head and neck in your medical history is a case-by-case conversation, since it changes how bone heals.

05

Willing to quit smoking, and committed to daily oral hygiene

Two lifestyle factors affect implant success more than almost anything else. Smoking narrows the small blood vessels in the gum, slows the fusion of the implant to the bone, and meaningfully raises the risk of failure both during healing and for years afterward. We ask you to stop before surgery, through the whole healing period, and ideally for good.Oral hygiene is what protects implants long term. An implant does not decay, but the gum and bone around it can become infected if plaque and tartar are allowed to build up, a condition called peri-implantitis. Brushing, flossing, and regular professional cleanings are what turn a well-placed implant into one that lasts for decades.

Dr. Meskin is a prosthodontist dedicated to one thing: replacing and restoring teeth so they look, feel, and function like the ones you were born with. He earned his Doctor of Dental Surgery degree and completed his specialty training in prosthodontics at NYU, then refined his implant work as an associate prosthodontist at ClearChoice, one of the largest dental implant networks in the country. Today he leads Hackensack Center for Dental Implants, where every case is planned in 3D, fabricated in an on-site lab, and designed around the patient sitting in front of him. ## Types of Dental Implants


Dental implants cover everything from replacing one tooth to rebuilding a whole mouth. Which option is right for you depends on how many teeth you are missing and the state of the ones around them.

Single Tooth Implant

One implant replaces one missing tooth, without touching the teeth on either side. The most conservative option when you are missing a single tooth.

Implant Bridge

Two implants can support a bridge of three or four teeth in a row, replacing a span without grinding down healthy neighboring teeth. The efficient choice when you are missing several teeth together.

All-on-X / Full-Arch Implants

Four to six implants support a fixed set of teeth that replaces an entire upper or lower arch. Used when most or all of the teeth in an arch are missing or failing.

Full-Mouth Rehabilitation

A phased plan that combines several implant and restorative treatments to rebuild the whole mouth. For patients whose issues have stacked up beyond a single treatment. Learn more about full-mouth rehabilitation


### Snap-In Overdenture


A removable denture that clips onto implants for far more hold than a traditional denture. Useful for some full-arch cases where a fixed set is not the right fit.

Book A Consultation


## How Dental Implants Are Done


Every implant treatment follows four clear stages, from your first evaluation to your final teeth


### Initial Consultation and Diagnostic Tests


Your first visit gives Dr. Meskin the information needed to plan treatment safely and accurately. We review your health history, examine your teeth and gums, and use 3D imaging to map the implant site.

A complete examination of your teeth, gums, bite, and missing-tooth site

A 3D cone beam scan to evaluate bone, nerves, and sinuses

Photographs or impressions to plan the appearance of your final teeth

A discussion of your goals, comfort options, and medical history

A clear treatment plan, timeline, and cost estimate


### Implant Placement


Once the site is ready, the implant is placed into the jawbone using the position established during 3D planning. Local anesthetic keeps the procedure comfortable, and sedation is available when appropriate.

Any required extraction, bone graft, or gum treatment is completed before or during placement.

The implant is guided into the planned position through a small opening in the gum.

A healing cap or temporary tooth may be provided, depending on the location and treatment plan.


### Healing


During the next few months, the implant bonds with the jawbone in a process called osseointegration. This creates a stable foundation for the final tooth. Most patients return to normal routines quickly while following simple instructions for diet, cleaning, and follow-up visits.


### Final Restoration


After the implant has fully healed, we capture a detailed impression and create the final crown, bridge, or full-arch restoration. Dr. Meskin checks the fit, bite, shape, and shade so the finished teeth feel comfortable and look natural.


## Real Patients, Real Stories


Hear from patients who rebuilt their entire smile and got their comfort and confidence back, in their own words.

View All Testimonials


## The Recovery Timeline


Recovery from dental implant surgery is usually milder than most people expect, and it happens in two layers. The visible part, the healing you notice around your gum, wraps up in about two weeks. The invisible part, where the implant fuses with the bone underneath, takes a few months and is what makes the finished tooth permanent. Understanding both layers is what makes the timeline make sense.


### A Typical Implant Recovery Timeline



#### Day 0


Placement. Minor soreness, soft foods, rest for the day.


#### Days 1 to 3


Peak swelling and soreness. Soft foods only. Usually milder than expected.


#### Days 4 to 7


Swelling drops off. Most people return to work.


#### Weeks 2 to 4


Stitches dissolve and gums heal. Still on a soft diet.


#### Months 1 to 3


The bone fuses to your implants. Keep protecting them with softer foods.


#### Months 3 to 6


Your final crown or teeth are placed. Back to a normal diet.


## Experience Exceptional Dental Care


Schedule your consultation today and see how different implant care can feel. At Hackensack Center for Dental Implants, your comfort, your confidence, and your smile always come first.


## Frequently Asked Questions


Am I too old for dental implants?

No. Age itself is not a barrier. Patients in their 70s, 80s, and beyond receive implants every year and heal well, provided general health supports it. What matters is your overall health and the quality of your bone, both of which are checked at your consultation.

Do dental implants hurt?

Most patients are surprised how comfortable it is. Placement is done under local anesthetic, and sedation is available for anyone who feels anxious. Any soreness afterward is usually managed with simple over-the-counter care.

How long does the implant process take?

From placement to your final tooth is usually a few months, because the implant needs time to fuse with the bone. Appointments themselves are short. Most of the timeline is quiet healing, not chair time.

How much do dental implants cost?

Cost depends on the type of case, from a single implant to a full-arch reconstruction. After your 3D scan you receive a clear written estimate with no surprises, plus financing options that spread the cost into monthly payments.

Full cost breakdown →

What if I do not have enough bone?

You may still qualify. Focused bone grafts can rebuild sites where the bone has shrunk, and angled implant designs like All-on-4 are built to work with limited bone. A 3D scan is the only way to know for certain, and many patients who were told no elsewhere still qualify here.

How long do dental implants last?

With good hygiene and regular check-ups, the implant itself can last for decades, often for life. The crown on top is durable and can be maintained or replaced over the years if needed.

Do you offer financing?

Yes. We will find a way. We try every avenue, and our dedicated team of treatment coordinators will help you find a plan that fits. We work with Cherry, HFD, Proceed, and CareCredit, and we verify any insurance benefits up front.

# Dental Implant FAQs



## Frequently Asked Questions


Do dental implants hurt?

The procedure itself is painless. Your mouth is fully numbed before anything begins, and sedation is available up to IV level. Afterward, soreness is usually mild, peaks around days one to three, and most patients manage it with over-the-counter pain relief. Most people describe the whole experience as far easier than they expected.

Will I have temporary teeth during healing?

In most cases, yes. For full-arch treatment, most patients leave with fixed temporary teeth the same day. For a single implant in a visible area, a temporary solution keeps you smiling while the implant heals. You are never sent home with a gap.

Do dental implants feel like real teeth?

Yes. Once fully healed and restored, most patients cannot tell the difference. They are fixed in place, so there is nothing to remove, no adhesive, and no slipping.

How long do dental implants last?

With proper care, dental implants can last a lifetime. The titanium implant integrates permanently with your bone. The crown or bridge on top is designed to last many years and can be replaced without disturbing the implant.

How do I care for my implants?

The same way you care for natural teeth: brush twice a day, floss daily, and keep up with regular check-ups. Dr. Meskin and the team schedule maintenance visits to keep everything healthy long term.

Will I need to miss work?

A single implant may only need a day. Full-arch surgery typically means a few days of rest, with most patients back to work within four to seven days. Your timeline is discussed in advance so you can plan around it.

What if I am missing a lot of teeth?

We treat everything from a single missing tooth to the complete loss of all teeth in one or both arches. All-on-X replaces a full arch with four to six implants, often with fixed teeth the same day.

I was told I do not have enough bone. Can I still get implants?

Often yes. Bone loss that would have ruled someone out years ago can frequently be worked around today with grafting and 3D-guided planning. A scan is the only way to know for sure.

What are the risks?

Dental implants have a very high success rate. As with any surgical procedure, there is a small chance of complications. If an implant does not integrate, it can usually be replaced successfully. Every case is planned with 3D imaging to minimize risk.

Is sedation available?

Yes. We offer a full range of sedation up to IV level. Your health history and suitability are evaluated before any sedation is recommended, and you are monitored continuously throughout.

How much do dental implants cost?

It depends on the treatment. A single tooth implant starts at $3,599, an implant bridge at $8,999, and full-arch All-on-X at $13,999 per arch. You receive a clear written estimate at your consultation.

Do you offer financing?

Yes. We work with Cherry, HFD, Proceed, and CareCredit. Our treatment coordinators will help you find a plan that fits, and we verify any insurance benefits up front.

Why see a prosthodontist for implants?

A prosthodontist completes years of specialty training focused entirely on replacing and restoring teeth. For full-arch, cosmetic, or complex cases, that depth of training means a more predictable, natural-looking result.

# Our Technology


Modern implant and restorative work depends on precision, and precision depends on the tools. At Hackensack Center, we invest in the equipment that lets Dr. Meskin diagnose more accurately, plan every case in detail, and finish treatment with a level of fit and comfort that older systems cannot match.

JUMP TO SECTION:

Show sections

1. On-Site Dental Lab2. 3D Printers3. 3D Imaging (Cone Beam CT)4. Photogrammetry5. CAD / CAM6. Intra-Oral Camera7. Intra-Oral Scanner8. Digital X-Ray


## On-Site Dental Lab


Most dental practices ship your crown, bridge, or full-arch restoration to an outside lab and wait weeks for it to come back. We do it in-house. Dr. Meskin works alongside the lab technician in the same room, adjusting your case together instead of sending it out and hoping the fit is right when it returns.

Faster turnaround, including same-day restorations where appropriate

Direct communication between the doctor and the lab, so no detail gets lost

Custom shade and shape matching done with your teeth in front of us, not from a photo


## 3D Printers


An in-office 3D printer produces the physical parts of your case on demand. Surgical guides that translate the 3D plan for your implant surgery into a precise physical template. Temporary teeth so you never leave with a gap. Study models used to try in and refine your final restoration before it is made permanent.

Custom surgical guides printed to make implant placement more precise

Same-day temporary teeth built to fit while your final work is being made

Accurate physical models for try-in and adjustment before anything permanent


## 3D Imaging (Cone Beam CT)


A cone beam CT scan captures a full three-dimensional view of your teeth, jaw, and the structures around them in a single quick pass. For implant work, this is the most important piece of technology in the office. Every implant Dr. Meskin places is planned against your actual anatomy, not against a flat picture of it.

Every implant planned in 3D around your bone, nerves, and sinuses

Bone quantity and quality measured precisely, so we know what your site can hold

Painless, quick, and delivered at a fraction of the radiation of a medical CT scan


## Photogrammetry


Photogrammetry uses a specialized camera to capture the exact 3D position of your implants down to a fraction of a millimeter. For full-arch cases like All-on-X, that level of precision is the difference between a restoration that fits comfortably from day one and one that has to come back for adjustment after adjustment.

Captures implant position with far greater accuracy than traditional impressions

Especially important for full-arch cases, where the smallest error compounds across every tooth

Fewer follow-up visits to adjust the fit of your final teeth


## CAD / CAM


CAD/CAM combines computer design with automated manufacturing to produce restorations with a precision the human hand cannot match. Your crown, bridge, or veneer is designed digitally against a scan of your mouth, then milled from a solid block of ceramic to those exact specifications.

Fit and finish designed digitally, milled to exact specifications

Solid ceramic construction that is stronger and more natural-looking than layered materials

Many restorations can be finished in-house without shipping out and waiting


## Intra-Oral Camera


A small, pen-shaped camera reaches areas of your mouth that a regular mirror cannot show clearly and puts the images up on a screen so you can see them too. It turns your visit into a conversation, because you see exactly what Dr. Meskin sees when he explains what a tooth needs.

Detailed views of cracks, wear, and old restorations that a mirror misses

Real-time images on screen, so you understand what is happening in your own mouth

Better documentation for your records and insurance claims


## Intra-Oral Scanner


A digital scanner replaces the tray of putty most people remember from old impressions. A small wand captures a full 3D image of your teeth in a few minutes, comfortable enough that patients often do not realize the impression is finished. The scan feeds straight into the plan for your crown, bridge, or implant restoration.

No more gagging on impression putty or waiting for it to set

Fully digital, so your case moves straight to the lab without shipping delays

More accurate impressions, especially for implant crowns and bridges


## Digital X-Ray


Digital sensors capture detailed images of your teeth almost instantly, with a fraction of the radiation of traditional film. Because the images appear on screen right away, Dr. Meskin can point directly to what he sees and explain it, rather than sending you home to wait for results.

Roughly 90 percent less radiation than older film-based systems

Images available on screen within seconds

Enhanced clarity for earlier detection of decay, cracks, and hidden infection


## Ready to Experience State of the Art Dental Care for Yourself?


Better tools mean less time in the chair, more accurate work, and results built to last. Here is what that adds up to at your visit.

Enhanced Diagnostics: 3D imaging and intra-oral cameras find problems older tools miss, so we can catch them earlier and treat them more conservatively.

Comfortable Experience: Digital scanning, laser tools, and precise printed guides cut both the number of visits and the discomfort at each one.

Lasting Results: Every implant planned in 3D, every crown milled to fit, every restoration matched by hand. Work that fits right, lasts.

## Frequently Asked Questions


Am I too old for dental implants?

No. Age itself is not a barrier. Patients in their 70s, 80s, and beyond receive implants every year and heal well, provided general health supports it. What matters is your overall health and the quality of your bone, both of which are checked at your consultation.

Do dental implants hurt?

Most patients are surprised how comfortable it is. Placement is done under local anesthetic, and sedation is available for anyone who feels anxious. Any soreness afterward is usually managed with simple over-the-counter care.

How long does the implant process take?

From placement to your final tooth is usually a few months, because the implant needs time to fuse with the bone. Appointments themselves are short. Most of the timeline is quiet healing, not chair time.

How much do dental implants cost?

Cost depends on the type of case, from a single implant to a full-arch reconstruction. After your 3D scan you receive a clear written estimate with no surprises, plus financing options that spread the cost into monthly payments.

Full cost breakdown →

What if I do not have enough bone?

You may still qualify. Focused bone grafts can rebuild sites where the bone has shrunk, and angled implant designs like All-on-4 are built to work with limited bone. A 3D scan is the only way to know for certain, and many patients who were told no elsewhere still qualify here.

How long do dental implants last?

With good hygiene and regular check-ups, the implant itself can last for decades, often for life. The crown on top is durable and can be maintained or replaced over the years if needed.

Do you offer financing?

Yes. We will find a way. We try every avenue, and our dedicated team of treatment coordinators will help you find a plan that fits. We work with Cherry, HFD, Proceed, and CareCredit, and we verify any insurance benefits up front.

# HIPAA DISCLOSURE


Effective Date: September 28, 2026

This Notice of Privacy Practices applies to Aesthetic Dental Center of Hackensack, LLC DBA Hackensack Center for Dental Implants (“Hackensack Center,” “we,” “us,” or “our”). For information about how we handle information collected through our website and other communications, please see our Privacy Policy.

Your Information. Your Rights. Our Responsibilities.

This notice describes how medical information about you may be used and disclosed and how you can get access to this information. Please review it carefully.

Aesthetic Dental Center of Hackensack, LLC

DBA Hackensack Center for Dental Implants

163 Main Street, Suite A1

Hackensack, NJ 07601

Phone: (201) 488-8866


## YOUR RIGHTS


You have the right to:

Get a copy of your paper or electronic medical record

Correct your paper or electronic medical record

Request confidential communication

Ask us to limit the information we share

Get a list of those with whom we’ve shared your information

Get a copy of this privacy notice

Choose someone to act for you

File a complaint if you believe your privacy rights have been violated


## YOUR CHOICES


You have some choices in the way that we use and share information as we:

Tell family and friends about your condition

Provide disaster relief

Include you in a hospital directory

Provide mental health care

Market our services and sell your information

Raise funds


## OUR USES AND DISCLOSURES


We may use and share your information as we:

Treat you

Run our organization

Bill for your services

Help with public health and safety issues

Do research

Comply with the law

Respond to organ and tissue donation requests

Work with a medical examiner or funeral director

Address workers’ compensation, law enforcement, and other government requests

Respond to lawsuits and legal actions


## YOUR RIGHTS


When it comes to your health information, you have certain rights. This section explains your rights and some of our responsibilities to help you.


### Get an electronic or paper copy of your medical record


You can ask to see or get an electronic or paper copy of your medical record and other health information we have about you. Ask us how to do this.

We will provide a copy or a summary of your health information, usually within 30 days of your request. We may charge a reasonable, cost-based fee.


### Ask us to correct your medical record


You can ask us to correct health information about you that you think is incorrect or incomplete. Ask us how to do this.

We may say “no” to your request, but we’ll tell you why in writing within 60 days.


### Request confidential communications


You can ask us to contact you in a specific way (for example, home or office phone) or to send mail to a different address.

We will say “yes” to all reasonable requests.


### Ask us to limit what we use or share


You can ask us not to use or share certain health information for treatment, payment, or our operations. We are not required to agree to your request, and we may say “no” if it would affect your care.

If you pay for a service or health care item out-of-pocket in full, you can ask us not to share that information for the purpose of payment or our operations with your health insurer. We will say “yes” unless a law requires us to share that information.


### Get a list of those with whom we’ve shared information


You can ask for a list (accounting) of the times we’ve shared your health information for six years prior to the date you ask, who we shared it with, and why.

We will include all the disclosures except for those about treatment, payment, and health care operations, and certain other disclosures (such as any you asked us to make). We’ll provide one accounting a year for free but will charge a reasonable, cost-based fee if you ask for another one within 12 months.


### Get a copy of this privacy notice


You can ask for a paper copy of this notice at any time, even if you have agreed to receive the notice electronically. We will provide you with a paper copy promptly.


### Choose someone to act for you


If you have given someone medical power of attorney or if someone is your legal guardian, that person can exercise your rights and make choices about your health information.

We will make sure the person has this authority and can act for you before we take any action.


### File a complaint if you feel your rights are violated


You can complain if you feel we have violated your rights by contacting us using the contact information at the top of this notice.

You can file a complaint with the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Office for Civil Rights by sending a letter to 200 Independence Avenue, S.W., Washington, D.C. 20201, calling 1-877-696-6775, or visiting www.hhs.gov/ocr/privacy/hipaa/complaints/

We will not retaliate against you for filing a complaint.


## YOUR CHOICES


For certain health information, you can tell us your choices about what we share. If you have a clear preference for how we share your information in the situations described below, talk to us. Tell us what you want us to do, and we will follow your instructions.

In these cases, you have both the right and choice to tell us to:

Share information with your family, close friends, or others involved in your care

Share information in a disaster relief situation

Include your information in a hospital directory

If you are not able to tell us your preference, for example if you are unconscious, we may go ahead and share your information if we believe it is in your best interest. We may also share your information when needed to lessen a serious and imminent threat to health or safety.

In these cases we never share your information unless you give us written permission:

Marketing purposes

Sale of your information

Most sharing of psychotherapy notes

In the case of fundraising:

We may contact you for fundraising efforts, but you can tell us not to contact you again.


## OUR USES AND DISCLOSURES


How do we typically use or share your health information?

We typically use or share your health information in the following ways.


### Treat you


We can use your health information and share it with other professionals who are treating you.

Example: A doctor treating you for an injury asks another doctor about your overall health condition.


### Run our organization


We can use and share your health information to run our practice, improve your care, and contact you when necessary.

Example: We use health information about you to manage your treatment and services.


### Bill for your services


We can use and share your health information to bill and get payment from health plans or other entities.

Example: We give information about you to your health insurance plan so it will pay for your services.


## HOW ELSE CAN WE USE OR SHARE YOUR HEALTH INFORMATION?


We are allowed or required to share your information in other ways – usually in ways that contribute to the public good, such as public health and research. We have to meet many conditions in the law before we can share your information for these purposes. For more information see: www.hhs.gov/ocr/privacy/hipaa/understanding/consumers/index.html.


### Help with public health and safety issues


We can share health information about you for certain situations such as:

Preventing disease

Helping with product recalls

Reporting adverse reactions to medications

Reporting suspected abuse, neglect, or domestic violence

Preventing or reducing a serious threat to anyone’s health or safety


### Do research


We can use or share your information for health research.


### Comply with the law


We will share information about you if state or federal laws require it, including with the Department of Health and Human Services if it wants to see that we’re complying with federal privacy law.


### Respond to organ and tissue donation requests


We can share health information about you with organ procurement organizations.


### Work with a medical examiner or funeral director


We can share health information with a coroner, medical examiner, or funeral director when an individual dies.


### Address workers’ compensation, law enforcement, and other government requests


We can use or share health information about you:

For workers’ compensation claims

For law enforcement purposes or with a law enforcement official

With health oversight agencies for activities authorized by law

For special government functions such as military, national security, and presidential protective services


### Respond to lawsuits and legal actions


We can share health information about you in response to a court or administrative order, or in response to a subpoena.


## REDISCLOSURE ACCORDING TO HIPAA


When you consent to uses and disclosures for all future treatment and payment purposes and to run our business, we may share your information with other substance use disorder treatment programs, doctors’ offices, and health care businesses for those activities. If the person who receives it is subject to HIPAA, then they are allowed to use and share your information again without your consent for the purposes that HIPAA allows. Your information still cannot be used in legal proceedings against you unless (1) you consent or (2) based on a Part 2 court order and a subpoena (or similar legal requirement).


## OUR RESPONSIBILITIES


We are required by law to maintain the privacy and security of your protected health information.

We will let you know promptly if a breach occurs that may have compromised the privacy or security of your information.

We must follow the duties and privacy practices described in this notice and give you a copy of it.

We will not use or share your information other than as described here unless you tell us we can in writing. If you tell us we can, you may change your mind at any time. Let us know in writing if you change your mind.

For more information see: www.hhs.gov/ocr/privacy/hipaa/understanding/consumers/noticepp.html.


## CHANGES TO THE TERMS OF THIS NOTICE


We can change the terms of this notice, and the changes will apply to all information we have about you. The new notice will be available upon request, in our office, and on our web site.

# All-On-X Recovery: What To Expect The Day After Same-Day Teeth Surgery


By DR. ALAN MESKIN

Updated On:

August 22, 2026


## Contents


Text Link

You did it. You walked into Hackensack Center for Dental Implants this morning with failing teeth or a worn-out denture, and you are walking out with a complete set of fixed teeth in your mouth. All-On-X same-day teeth surgery is one of the most transformative procedures in modern dentistry, and the next 24 to 48 hours of recovery set the foundation for your long-term success.

This guide walks you through exactly what to expect after your All-On-X procedure with Dr. Meskin, hour by hour and day by day for the critical first 2 days. Following these instructions carefully will keep you comfortable, protect your new teeth, and help your implants integrate successfully with your bone.


## The Drive Home: Hours 0 to 4


You had IV sedation. You will be groggy, sleepy, and possibly emotional as the medication wears off. Your driver should plan to stay with you for the next 24 hours, or arrange for a family member to take over once you are home.


### What To Expect


Your mouth will feel numb for 2 to 4 more hours from local anesthesia

You may feel some mild bleeding or pink saliva, which is normal

Your lips and cheeks may feel swollen or puffy

You will have a complete set of temporary teeth attached to your implants already

You may feel a slight strange sensation as you adjust to the new fixed teeth


### Right When You Get Home


Rest in a recliner or propped up with pillows, head elevated

Apply ice packs to your cheeks (20 minutes on, 20 minutes off) for the next 24 hours

Take prescribed pain medication BEFORE the numbness fully wears off

Sip cool water and clear liquids slowly, no straws

Do not look in the mirror for a thorough inspection yet, you will feel more swollen than you actually look

Rest is the most important thing during the first 24 hours. Your body is healing from a significant procedure and needs your attention.


## The First Evening: Hours 4 to 12


By the evening of your surgery day, the sedation will be mostly out of your system but you should still rest. Light activity around the house is fine, but no driving, no major decisions, and no signing legal documents until tomorrow.


### What To Eat


For the first 24 hours, stick to room-temperature soft liquids and very soft foods that require no chewing. Good options:

Cool smoothies (no straw, sip from the cup)

Cold yogurt

Lukewarm soup or broth

Applesauce

Pudding or mashed banana

Avoid hot temperatures for the first 24 hours because the heat can increase bleeding. Avoid anything that requires chewing. Your new teeth are functional but need 3 to 5 months for the implants underneath to fully integrate with bone, and putting heavy chewing pressure on them too soon can disrupt healing.


### Pain Management


Take prescribed pain medication on a schedule for the first 48 to 72 hours, not just when pain becomes severe. Staying ahead of pain is much easier than catching up to it. Most patients report manageable discomfort, more like a dull ache than sharp pain, especially when on schedule with their medication.


## Day 1: The First 24 Hours


Day 1 is the most important for setting up successful long-term healing. Your job today is simple: rest, manage swelling, take medications on schedule, and protect your new teeth.


### Morning of Day 1


You may wake up with more swelling than you went to bed with. This is completely normal. Swelling peaks at 48 to 72 hours, so today and tomorrow will feel worse than today before things improve.

Continue ice packs every 20 minutes throughout the day. Take pain medication on schedule. Sip cool water and soft foods throughout the day to stay hydrated and nourished.


### Salt Water Rinses Start Today


Beginning 24 hours after surgery, start gentle salt water rinses. Mix 1/2 teaspoon of salt in 8 ounces of warm water. Gently swish, then let the water drip out of your mouth rather than spitting forcefully. Rinse 3 to 4 times per day, especially after eating anything. Do not use commercial mouthwash, which contains alcohol that can irritate the surgical sites.


### Do Not Brush Your New Teeth Yet


Do not brush your healing teeth or surgical sites for the first 24 hours. After 24 hours, you can use a soft toothbrush to gently brush the chewing surfaces of your healing teeth (the part that bites food), but avoid the gum line until your follow-up visit.

The first 10 to 14 days require a soft diet. Yogurt, smoothies, scrambled eggs, soft pasta, and well-cooked vegetables are your best friends.


## Day 2: When Things Get Worse Before Better


Most patients report that day 2 and day 3 are actually more uncomfortable than the day of surgery itself. This is when swelling peaks and bruising may appear on the cheeks or jaw. This is normal and not a sign that anything is wrong.


### Continue The Routine


Ice packs every 20 minutes for any remaining swelling

Pain medication on schedule, not just when it hurts

Salt water rinses 3 to 4 times per day

Soft food diet, no chewing yet

Rest as much as possible, light walking around the house is fine


### What You Can Eat on Day 2


By day 2 you can introduce more variety while still avoiding chewing:

Soft scrambled eggs

Cottage cheese

Mashed potatoes (lukewarm, not hot)

Oatmeal or cream of wheat

Soft pasta with light sauce

Soft fish (tilapia, cod)

Refried beans

Avocado

Continue avoiding hot temperatures, hard or crunchy foods, anything seedy, and chewy meats. Your new teeth are temporary and not strong enough for normal chewing yet.


## The Soft Food Diet: Weeks 1 to 12


For the first 12 weeks after All-On-X surgery, you are on a progressive soft food diet. The implants underneath your new teeth are fusing with your jawbone, and heavy chewing pressure during this critical period can disrupt the bond.

Week 1 to 2: Liquids and very soft foods only, no chewing

Week 3 to 6: Soft foods that require gentle chewing, no hard or crunchy

Week 7 to 12: Most foods are fine, but still avoid extremely hard items

Week 12 onward: Once implants are fully integrated, return to normal diet

Once you receive your final permanent zirconia bridge at the 3 to 5 month mark, you can eat nearly everything that natural teeth can eat. Most patients describe biting into their first apple or steak as one of the most emotional moments of their treatment.


## When To Call Us


Call Hackensack Center for Dental Implants at (201) 488-8866 immediately if you experience:

Bleeding that does not stop after 4 hours of pressure

Severe pain not controlled by prescribed medication

Swelling that worsens after day 4 instead of improving

Fever above 101 degrees Fahrenheit

The temporary bridge becomes loose, broken, or feels different

Pus or foul taste from any surgical site

Numbness in the lip, tongue, or chin that does not resolve within 48 hours


## Your First Follow-Up Visit


You will return to see Dr. Meskin at 1 to 2 weeks after surgery for your first follow-up. We check healing progress, remove any non-dissolving stitches, adjust your temporary bridge if needed, and answer questions. Visit our What To Expect page for a full overview of the All-On-X timeline.

In Conclusion

The first 48 hours after All-On-X surgery are the most demanding of your recovery, but they are also temporary. With rest, ice packs, pain medication on schedule, soft foods, and gentle salt water rinses, most patients move through the first 2 days without major issues.

The key is to be patient with yourself and trust the process. Your new teeth are already in your mouth, your implants are integrating below the surface, and in 3 to 5 months you will return for your final permanent zirconia bridge and resume eating everything you love.


# Frequently Asked Questions


How long is recovery after All-On-X same-day teeth surgery?

Most All-On-X patients return to light daily activities within 3 to 5 days after surgery. The gum tissue heals within 2 to 3 weeks, and the implants fully integrate with the jawbone over the next 3 to 5 months. Your final permanent zirconia bridge replaces the temporary bridge at the 3 to 5 month mark, completing your full recovery.

What can I eat after All-On-X surgery?

For the first 24 hours, stick to cool liquids and very soft foods like smoothies, yogurt, applesauce, pudding, and lukewarm soup with no chewing. By day 2, add soft scrambled eggs, cottage cheese, mashed potatoes, oatmeal, soft pasta, soft fish, refried beans, and avocado. Avoid hot temperatures, hard or crunchy foods, and chewing for the first 12 weeks while implants integrate.

Will the temporary bridge fall out after All-On-X surgery?

No. Your temporary bridge is securely attached to your implants the day of surgery and is designed to stay in place for the full 3 to 5 month healing period. It is much stronger than a removable denture. However, you should still avoid hard or chewy foods that could put excessive pressure on the bridge. If the bridge becomes loose or breaks, contact our office immediately.

How painful is All-On-X recovery?

Most patients describe All-On-X recovery as more uncomfortable than painful, similar to having multiple teeth extracted. Discomfort peaks at 48 to 72 hours after surgery and is well controlled with prescribed pain medication. Take medication on schedule for the first 2 to 3 days rather than waiting until pain becomes severe. Most patients transition to over-the-counter ibuprofen by day 4 or 5.

When can I brush my All-On-X teeth?

Do not brush your healing teeth for the first 24 hours after surgery. Starting on day 2, you can use a soft toothbrush to gently brush the chewing surfaces of your temporary teeth, avoiding the gum line and surgical sites. Continue salt water rinses 3 to 4 times per day. After your first follow-up visit, Dr. Alan Meskin will give you specific instructions for cleaning around your implants.

When can I drink alcohol after All-On-X surgery?

Avoid alcohol for at least 72 hours after All-On-X surgery. Alcohol can interfere with healing, interact with prescribed medications, and increase bleeding. After 72 hours, light alcohol consumption is generally fine, but avoid heavy drinking for the first 2 weeks. Do not drink alcohol while taking prescription pain medication or opioids.

Can I smoke after All-On-X surgery?

No. Smoking significantly increases the risk of implant failure and is particularly damaging during the 3 to 5 month osseointegration period when your implants are fusing with your bone. Smokers have 2 to 3 times the implant failure rate compared to non-smokers. We strongly recommend quitting at least 2 weeks before surgery and avoiding all tobacco products for at least 4 weeks after.

Why does my swelling get worse on day 2 and 3?

This is completely normal. Swelling typically peaks at 48 to 72 hours after All-On-X surgery and then gradually subsides over the following week. Apply ice packs to your cheeks (20 minutes on, 20 minutes off) during the first 24 hours, then switch to warm compresses on day 3 if swelling lingers. If swelling worsens after day 4 instead of improving, contact our office.

How do I clean my All-On-X temporary teeth?

After the first 24 hours, gently brush the chewing surfaces of your temporary bridge with a soft toothbrush. Continue salt water rinses 3 to 4 times per day. Avoid the gum line and surgical sites during the first 2 weeks. Once cleared at your follow-up visit, you will receive specific instructions for using an interdental brush or water flosser to clean around and underneath the bridge.

When can I return to work after All-On-X surgery?

Most patients with desk jobs return to work 3 to 5 days after All-On-X surgery, although some patients prefer to take a full week off to rest and recover comfortably. Avoid jobs that require heavy physical activity, public speaking, or food service for at least 7 days. Plan to take at least 2 to 3 days off work as a minimum, and consider working from home if possible for the first week.

DR. ALAN MESKIN

Dr. Alan Meskin, DDS, is a prosthodontist and the founder of Hackensack Center for Dental Implants. NYU-trained in both dentistry and the prosthodontics specialty, he focuses on dental implants, full-mouth reconstruction, and cosmetic smile design, including the complex cases many general offices refer out. His approach is straightforward: listen first, plan every case in 3D before it begins, and design each smile in our on-site lab to look and function like the patient's own teeth.

# All-On-X vs Traditional Dentures: Which Is Right For You in 2026?


By DR. ALAN MESKIN

Updated On:

August 22, 2026


## Contents


Text Link

If you are missing most or all of your teeth in an arch, you have two main paths forward in modern dentistry: traditional removable dentures or All-On-X full-arch dental implants. Both replace missing teeth. Both restore your smile cosmetically. But the day-to-day experience of living with one versus the other could not be more different.

This guide compares All-On-X and traditional dentures honestly across the factors that actually matter to patients: cost over time, comfort, eating ability, speech, bone preservation, lifespan, and maintenance. By the end, you will have a clear picture of which option fits your priorities, your budget, and your lifestyle.


## What Is the Difference Between All-On-X and Traditional Dentures?


Traditional dentures are removable prosthetic teeth that rest on top of your gums. They are held in place by suction, denture adhesive, or both. Patients take them out at night for cleaning and to give the gums a rest.

All-On-X dental implants are permanent, non-removable replacement teeth supported by 4 to 8 titanium implants surgically placed in your jawbone. The implants fuse with your bone over 3 to 5 months and act as artificial tooth roots, supporting a fixed zirconia bridge that you brush and floss just like natural teeth.

The fundamental difference: dentures sit on your gums. All-On-X teeth are anchored into your bone. That single distinction drives every other difference between the two options.

Traditional dentures sit on top of your gums and rely on suction or adhesive. All-On-X implants are anchored permanently into your jawbone.


## Cost Comparison: Upfront vs Long-Term


Traditional dentures usually have a lower initial cost. All-On-X requires a greater upfront investment because treatment includes implant placement, surgery, and a fixed restoration. The exact cost depends on your bone condition, number of implants, sedation needs, and final restoration materials.

Long-term denture expenses may include adjustments, relines, repairs, adhesives, and periodic replacement. All-On-X may involve fewer routine replacement expenses, but the bridge and other restorative components can still require professional maintenance, repair, or eventual replacement.

A fair comparison should use itemized estimates for both options based on your specific needs. Neither treatment is guaranteed to be less expensive over a lifetime. Our team will explain the immediate and anticipated long-term costs during your consultation.

For a complete pricing breakdown and financing options, visit our Cost of Dental Implants page.


## Eating: What You Can and Cannot Chew


This is where the two options diverge most dramatically.

Traditional dentures restore about 25% of your natural biting force. Steaks, raw vegetables, crusty bread, apples, corn on the cob, and many nuts become difficult or impossible. Many denture wearers gradually adapt their diet to softer foods, which can lead to nutritional gaps over time.

All-On-X restores roughly 90% of natural biting force because the implants transmit pressure directly into your jawbone, just like natural teeth. Patients return to eating steak, raw apples, nuts, and corn on the cob the same way they did before tooth loss. For many All-On-X patients, the first apple they eat in years is one of the most emotional moments of their treatment.

Even warm soft meals taste better when you can enjoy them without slipping dentures or sore gums getting in the way.


## Speech: Slurring and Clicking


Traditional dentures can shift during speech, causing clicking sounds, slurred consonants, and the constant need to readjust them with the tongue. Many denture wearers report feeling self-conscious about speaking in meetings, social gatherings, or on the phone.

All-On-X teeth do not move. They are bolted into your jaw. Speech sounds exactly like it did with natural teeth, with no clicking, no slipping, and no readjustment. Patients often describe the relief of forgetting they have implants at all.


## Bone Preservation: The Hidden Long-Term Cost of Dentures


This is the factor most denture wearers do not understand until it is too late.

Your jawbone is stimulated by the pressure of chewing transmitted through tooth roots. When natural teeth are removed and replaced with dentures, the bone stops receiving that stimulation. Over time, the jawbone resorbs (shrinks) at a rate of about 25% in the first year and continues shrinking gradually for the rest of your life.

This is why long-term denture wearers develop the "sunken in" facial appearance and why dentures need to be relined repeatedly. The bone supporting them is literally disappearing underneath.

All-On-X stops bone loss entirely. The implants act like natural tooth roots, transmitting chewing pressure into the bone and preserving its volume and density indefinitely. For patients who have already lost significant bone, we offer zygomatic implants as an alternative that bypasses the missing bone entirely.


## Lifespan and Maintenance


Traditional dentures: 5 to 7 years between replacements. Daily removal for cleaning, overnight soak in denture solution, regular relines as bone shrinks, and the constant management of slippage.

All-On-X: All-On-X implants and restorations are designed for long-term use, but their longevity varies by patient health, implant integration, oral hygiene, bite forces, and professional maintenance. The implants may remain stable for many years, while the bridge can eventually require repair or replacement due to normal wear. Brush daily, clean underneath the bridge as instructed, and attend the professional maintenance visits recommended by your dental team.


## Who Should Choose Each Option?


Traditional dentures may be the right choice if you:

Have severe health conditions that make surgery risky

Need an immediate solution while saving for permanent treatment

Genuinely cannot accommodate implants even with bone grafting or zygomatic alternatives

Prefer removable prosthetics for personal reasons

All-On-X is the better choice if you:

Want to eat all the foods you love without restriction

Are tired of denture slippage, adhesives, and the constant management

Want to preserve your jawbone and facial structure for the long term

Want a permanent solution you do not have to think about every day

For patients who want something between the two, our implant-supported snap-on dentures offer many of the benefits of All-On-X at a lower price point.

In Conclusion

The choice between All-On-X and traditional dentures is not only about initial cost. It also depends on your health, bone condition, treatment goals, lifestyle, and willingness to maintain the restoration.

Dentures generally cost less initially but require daily removal and ongoing adjustments. All-On-X requires surgery and a greater upfront investment but provides fixed teeth and stronger chewing function for suitable candidates. A consultation and 3D CBCT evaluation with Dr. Alan Meskin can help determine which option best fits your clinical needs and goals.


# Frequently Asked Questions


What is the main difference between All-On-X and traditional dentures?

Traditional dentures rest on top of your gums and are held in place by suction or adhesive. All-On-X dental implants are permanently anchored into your jawbone with 4 to 8 titanium implants supporting a fixed zirconia bridge. The fundamental difference is that dentures sit on gums while All-On-X is bolted into bone, which drives every other difference in comfort, eating, speech, and bone preservation.

Is All-On-X more expensive than traditional dentures over a lifetime?

All-On-X generally has a higher initial cost than traditional dentures. However, denture owners may have continuing expenses for relines, adjustments, adhesives, repairs, and replacement. All-On-X restorations also require professional maintenance and can eventually need repair or replacement. The total long-term cost depends on the patient and treatment plan, so request itemized estimates for both options before deciding.

Can I eat normally with traditional dentures?

Traditional dentures restore about 25% of your natural biting force, which makes steak, raw vegetables, crusty bread, apples, corn on the cob, and many nuts difficult or impossible to chew. Many denture wearers gradually adapt to softer foods, which can lead to nutritional gaps. All-On-X restores roughly 90% of natural biting force, so most foods can be eaten normally.

Do dentures cause bone loss?

Yes. When natural teeth are removed and replaced with dentures, the jawbone stops receiving chewing stimulation and resorbs about 25% in the first year, then continues shrinking gradually. This is why long-term denture wearers develop a sunken facial appearance and need frequent denture relines. All-On-X stops bone loss entirely because the implants stimulate the bone like natural tooth roots.

How long do All-On-X dental implants last compared to dentures?

All-On-X implants are intended as a long-term treatment, but longevity depends on implant integration, general health, oral hygiene, bite forces, and maintenance. The bridge may eventually require repair or replacement because of normal wear. Traditional dentures generally require more frequent adjustments, relines, and replacement as the mouth and jaw change.

Will my speech change with dentures or All-On-X?

Traditional dentures can shift during speech, causing clicking sounds and slurred consonants, and many denture wearers report self-consciousness in social settings or on the phone. All-On-X teeth do not move because they are anchored in the jawbone, so speech sounds exactly like it did with natural teeth, with no clicking or slipping.

Can I get All-On-X if I have been wearing dentures for years?

Many long-term denture wearers can qualify for All-On-X, but eligibility depends on their remaining bone, oral health, medical history, and treatment goals. Some patients may need bone grafting or another advanced approach. A 3D CBCT evaluation allows the treatment team to assess your anatomy and recommend the safest appropriate option.

How do I clean All-On-X teeth compared to dentures?

All-On-X teeth are cleaned just like natural teeth with twice-daily brushing and flossing with a special threader, plus two professional cleanings per year. There is no removal, no overnight soaking, and no adhesive. Traditional dentures must be removed daily for cleaning, soaked overnight in denture solution, and adhesive must be applied each morning.

Is there an option between dentures and All-On-X?

Yes. Implant-supported removable dentures, sometimes called overdentures or snap-on dentures, use implants to stabilize a removable restoration. They can improve retention, chewing, and comfort compared with traditional dentures while remaining removable for cleaning. Pricing depends on the number of implants, bone condition, sedation needs, and restoration design.

How do I decide which option is right for me?

The best way to decide is through a consultation and 3D CBCT evaluation with Dr. Alan Meskin. Your bone quality, oral health, medical history, lifestyle, maintenance preferences, goals, and budget should all be considered. The recommended treatment should be based on your individual needs rather than assuming one option is appropriate for everyone.

Dr. Alan Meskin, DDS, is a prosthodontist and the founder of Hackensack Center for Dental Implants. NYU-trained in both dentistry and the prosthodontics specialty, he focuses on dental implants, full-mouth reconstruction, and cosmetic smile design, including the complex cases many general offices refer out. His approach is straightforward: listen first, plan every case in 3D before it begins, and design each smile in our on-site lab to look and function like the patient's own teeth.

# How Much Do Dental Implants Cost in Hackensack, NJ? A Complete 2026 Guide


By DR. ALAN MESKIN

Updated On:

August 22, 2026


## Contents


Text Link

If you are researching dental implants in Hackensack, NJ, the cost can be difficult to understand. Every patient has different clinical needs, and the final price may be affected by the number of implants, extractions, bone grafting, sedation, temporary teeth, and the design of the final restoration.

At Hackensack Center for Dental Implants, every patient receives an individualized treatment plan after a complete evaluation. This guide explains the factors that affect dental implant costs, what to look for in an itemized estimate, how insurance may contribute, and which financing options may be available.


## Dental Implant Costs in Hackensack, NJ: What to Expect


Here are our transparent published prices for 2026, listed from the most affordable option to the most premium:

Single-tooth implant: Pricing depends on whether the estimate includes the implant post, abutment, final crown, imaging, extraction, bone grafting, and sedation.

Implant-supported removable denture: Cost varies according to the number of implants, existing bone, denture design, and materials.

All-On-X full-arch treatment: Pricing depends on extractions, implant quantity, sedation, temporary teeth, and the final fixed restoration.

Fixed zirconia or FP1 restoration: Cost varies according to the implant foundation, prosthetic design, materials, and laboratory work.

Advanced bone-loss treatment: Patients requiring grafting or another advanced surgical approach receive a customized treatment estimate.

Compare implant estimates according to what is included—not only the advertised starting price. Ask whether the estimate covers imaging, extractions, grafting, sedation, temporary teeth, the final restoration, adjustments, and postoperative care. Hackensack Center provides an itemized treatment plan so you can understand each proposed service before proceeding.


## What Affects the Final Cost of Your Dental Implants?


The starting prices above cover the implants and final restoration for a standard case. Your individual treatment plan may include additional procedures that affect the total cost. These are the most common variables:


### Bone Grafting


Some patients need bone grafting before or during implant placement because the jawbone has changed after tooth loss or long-term denture use. The need for grafting, the type of graft, and its associated cost are determined after a clinical examination and 3D imaging. Any recommended grafting should appear as a separate item in your treatment estimate.


### Sinus Lift


For upper-arch implants near the sinus cavity, a sinus lift may be needed to create enough bone for stable implant placement. Sinus lifts typically add $1,500 to $2,500 to your treatment cost. For patients with severe upper-jaw bone loss who want to avoid sinus lifts entirely, zygomatic implants offer an alternative path.


### Tooth Extractions


If failing teeth must be removed before implant placement, extractions are typically billed separately at $150 to $400 per tooth. Insurance often covers extractions even when it does not cover the implant itself.


### Sedation Options


Sedation options are available to help patients remain comfortable during implant treatment. The recommended method depends on the procedure, medical history, anxiety level, and clinical team involved. Your treatment coordinator will explain the sedation plan and whether its cost is included or listed separately before treatment begins.

Our financial coordinator walks every patient through their personalized cost breakdown and financing options before treatment begins.


## How To Make Dental Implants Affordable in Hackensack, NJ


The published prices are just the starting point. Most of our patients pair partial insurance coverage with monthly financing to make implant treatment fit their budget. Here is how it works.


### Insurance Coverage


Most dental insurance plans classify the implant itself as cosmetic and offer limited direct coverage. However, many plans do contribute toward related procedures:

Tooth extractions before implant placement

Bone grafting and sinus lifts

The final crown or prosthetic restoration

Routine cleanings during your treatment journey

Our dedicated insurance coordinator verifies every patient's benefits before treatment and submits claims electronically on your behalf. Visit our Insurance & Financing page to learn more about how we maximize your coverage.


### Dental Implant Financing Options


We work with more financing partners than most dental practices in Arvada, including:

Cherry

HFD

Proceed

CareCredit

Financing availability, loan terms, interest rates, down payments, and monthly payments depend on the applicant and financing provider. Our treatment coordinators can explain the available programs and help qualified patients review their payment options.


### HSA and FSA Funds


Dental implants, including the surgery, abutment, and final crown, are typically eligible expenses under both Health Savings Accounts (HSA) and Flexible Spending Accounts (FSA). Our financial coordinator can provide all the documentation you need for reimbursement and help you maximize tax benefits.


## Why Our Pricing Is Different From the National Chains


Big-name implant chains carry overhead costs that small independent practices do not.

Franchise fees, television marketing, multi-location administration, and corporate profit margins all get passed on to patients in the form of higher prices and "upcharges" that turn the advertised price into a much larger final bill.

Hackensack Center for Dental Implants combines treatment planning, 3D imaging, restorative care, and an on-site dental lab within one coordinated practice. Dr. Alan Meskin and the treatment team create an individualized plan based on each patient’s anatomy, health, functional needs, and smile goals. Every estimate should clearly identify the proposed procedures and restorations.

For a complete walkthrough of what is and is not included in our prices, visit our dedicated Cost of Dental Implants page.

In Conclusion

Dental implant costs in Hackensack, NJ vary according to the number of missing teeth, available bone, surgical needs, sedation plan, temporary restoration, and final prosthetic design. The most reliable way to understand your cost is to receive a complete evaluation and an itemized treatment plan. Hackensack Center for Dental Implants offers complimentary consultations, and any diagnostic imaging or additional services should be explained before they are performed.


# Frequently Asked Questions


How much does a single dental implant cost in Hackensack, NJ?

Single-tooth implant pricing depends on whether treatment includes an extraction, bone grafting, imaging, sedation, implant placement, an abutment, and the final crown. After evaluating your needs, Hackensack Center will provide an itemized estimate showing what is included and which services, if any, are separate.

How much does All-On-X cost per arch in Hackensack, NJ?

All-On-X pricing varies according to the number of implants, extractions, available bone, sedation needs, temporary teeth, and the final restoration. Following a clinical and 3D evaluation, the treatment team will provide an itemized estimate explaining every proposed component.

Why do advertised full-arch implant prices vary so much?

Advertised prices may include different services and materials. Some estimates cover only surgery and temporary teeth, while others include imaging, extractions, sedation, implants, temporary teeth, and the final restoration. Always request a written, itemized estimate and confirm exactly what is included before comparing providers.

Does dental insurance cover dental implants in Hackensack, NJ?

Coverage varies by insurance plan. Some plans may contribute toward implant treatment or related services such as extractions, grafting, crowns, or routine care. Hackensack Center can verify your available benefits and submit eligible claims, but coverage and reimbursement are determined by the insurance carrier.

Can I finance dental implants with bad credit?

Financing approval depends on the lender, applicant, requested amount, and credit profile. Hackensack Center currently works with Cherry, HFD, Proceed, and CareCredit. Each provider has its own eligibility requirements and terms, so approval, interest rates, and monthly payments cannot be guaranteed.

What payment plans are available for dental implants?

Financing options are available through Cherry, HFD, Proceed, and CareCredit for qualified applicants. Terms, interest rates, down payments, and monthly payments vary. The treatment coordinator can help you review the programs currently available.

Are sedation options available for dental implant treatment?

Sedation options are available for appropriate patients. The recommended method and associated cost depend on the procedure, medical history, and treatment team. Your sedation plan and any related charges will be explained before treatment.

Can I use my HSA or FSA for dental implants?

Yes. Dental implants including the surgery, abutment, and final crown are typically eligible expenses under both Health Savings Accounts (HSA) and Flexible Spending Accounts (FSA). Our financial coordinator can provide all the documentation you need for reimbursement and help you structure payment to maximize tax benefits.

Is an implant consultation complimentary at Hackensack Center for Dental Implants?

Yes. Hackensack Center offers complimentary implant consultations. The team will discuss your concerns and treatment goals. Any diagnostic imaging or additional services and their associated costs should be explained before they are performed.

How does Hackensack Center prepare dental implant estimates?

Hackensack Center prepares an individualized treatment plan based on your anatomy, health, functional needs, and restorative goals. The estimate should identify the proposed procedures, temporary restoration, final restoration, sedation plan, laboratory work, and any additional services so you can understand the complete expected cost.
